nameStory: Gonium gets its name from the Greek word 'gonia,' meaning 'angle' or 'corner,' referring to the geometric way its cells arrange themselves in neat, flat colonies. The species name 'pectorale' means 'of the chest,' describing how the flat colony resembles a breastplate when viewed under a microscope.
description: Gonium is a tiny colonial green algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's strictly a microscope discovery! Each colony looks like a miniature green plate made up of 4 to 16 individual cells arranged in a perfectly flat pattern. These microscopic water-dwellers are actually plant-like organisms that swim around in ponds and streams using tiny whip-like tails called flagella. Though invisible to us, they're among the most common algae in New England's freshwater habitats.

idTips.label: Colony Shape
idTips.description: Flat, plate-like colonies that look like tiny green pancakes under the microscope, never forming spheres or chains

idTips.label: Cell Arrangement
idTips.description: Individual cells arranged in neat geometric patterns of 4, 8, or 16 cells per colony, like a perfectly organized green mosaic

idTips.label: Swimming Motion
idTips.description: Colonies glide smoothly through the water with coordinated movement, rotating gently as they travel

idTips.label: Cell Structure
idTips.description: Each cell has two flagella (whip-like tails) and a bright green chloroplast that gives the colony its emerald color

idTips.label: Size Scale
idTips.description: Entire colonies are microscopic, requiring at least 100x magnification to see clearly

habitat: Gonium thrives in New England's quiet freshwater environments - ponds, slow-moving streams, and the shallow edges of lakes where the water is still or barely moving. Look for it in nutrient-rich waters, often where fallen leaves or other organic matter provide food sources. It's particularly common in temporary pools and woodland ponds during warmer months.

seasonality.spring: Colonies become active as water temperatures rise, beginning their swimming and reproduction cycles in warming ponds and streams.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when colonies are most numerous and easiest to find in freshwater samples, actively reproducing both sexually and asexually.
seasonality.fall: Still present but less active as temperatures drop, forming resistant stages to survive the coming winter months.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant in frozen or near-freezing water, surviving as hardy resting cells until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Gonium is like a living bridge between single-celled and multicellular life - scientists study it to understand how complex organisms like us might have evolved from simple, one-celled ancestors millions of years ago!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, Gonium might be confused with Volvox or other colonial algae, but remember the 'flat pancake rule' - Gonium always forms flat plates while Volvox makes hollow spheres, and other colonial algae form chains or irregular clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Though called an 'algae,' Gonium is actually more closely related to plants than to seaweeds, belonging to the green algae group that gave rise to all land plants. The name can be tricky to pronounce - it's 'GO-nee-um,' with the emphasis on the first syllable.
compareHints: Since Gonium is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to its colonial relatives like Volvox and Eudorina. Unlike the hollow, soccer ball-like colonies of Volvox or the smaller, more irregular clusters of Eudorina, Gonium's flat, geometric arrangement of cells makes it unique among New England's colonial green algae.
